slides.0.title: Introducing Champagne
slides.0.subtitle: History and myth, UNESCO and the appellation today
slides.1.title: Why study Champagne?
slides.1.highlights.0.title: A topic in both D3 and D5
slides.1.highlights.0.content: In the WSET Diploma, Champagne is core to both D3 (the wines of France) and D5 (sparkling wines), so you need both the region and the traditional method
slides.1.highlights.1.title: 34,200 ha, 319 crus, 5 départements
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Comité Champagne key figures: about 34,200 ha of vines across 5 départements and 319 villages (crus)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: A marginal northern sparkling region
slides.1.highlights.2.content: The cool climate gives high-acid, lower-sugar base wines, exactly the raw material sparkling wine needs
slides.1.highlights.3.title: About 266 million bottles shipped in 2025
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Comité Champagne 2025 key figures: about 266.1 million bottles shipped; 2024 was 271.7 million (see the note on differing editions)
slides.1.content: Key figures are updated yearly. For producer counts, the 2023 edition lists 16,200 growers / 370 houses / 130 cooperatives, the 2024 edition 16,300 / 390 / 125 and the 2025 edition 16,460 / 410 / 120. We always state the year, and such figures are not tested.
slides.2.title: From Rome to the 17th century: wine first, bubbles later
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Planted by the Romans, famed for still wine in the Middle Ages
slides.2.highlights.0.content: The Romans first planted vines here; medieval Champagne was known for pale red and still wines that competed with Burgundy
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Coronations at Reims and wine
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Comité Champagne records French kings being crowned at Reims from 898 to 1825, tying Champagne to royalty and celebration
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Bubbles began as a "fault"
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Cold winters halted fermentation, and when spring warmed the bottled wine it started again and made bubbles, which people at first saw as a nuisance
slides.2.highlights.3.title: 1662: Merret's paper
slides.2.highlights.3.content: In 1662 England's Christopher Merret presented a paper to the Royal Society describing sugar-induced second fermentation, years before Dom Pérignon arrived at Hautvillers
slides.2.content: Bubbling wine was observed in many places. What set Champagne apart is that it was the first region to try to understand and control it.
slides.3.title: Myth versus fact: Dom Pérignon did not "invent Champagne"
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Myth: he invented Champagne
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Comité Champagne puts it plainly: Champagne was not invented by anyone. Crediting one monk is a later story
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Myth: "I am tasting the stars"
slides.3.highlights.1.content: This famous line is widely regarded as a 19th-century advertising invention, not something he said
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Fact: monk and cellar master
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Dom Pérignon (1638–1715) ran the cellars at Hautvillers Abbey from 1668, and his contribution lay in better pressing, blending and grape quality rather than inventing bubbles
slides.3.highlights.3.title: How to tell them apart
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Trust dated documents: Merret's 1662 paper predates his arrival, and it is generally held that he actually worked to avoid bubbles
slides.3.content: A tip for MW essays: for any "X invented Y" claim, find the dates and primary sources first. Myths can colour the background but cannot carry an argument.
slides.4.title: From the 19th century to today: industry, riots, delimitation and UNESCO
slides.4.highlights.0.title: 19th-century technology and the great houses
slides.4.highlights.0.content: The muselet wire cage (1844), riddling (traditionally linked to Veuve Clicquot) and dry Brut (from around the 1870s) turned Champagne into an exportable branded industry
slides.4.highlights.1.title: The 1911 Champagne riots
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Low grape prices, houses buying grapes from elsewhere and boundary disputes led to riots in the Marne in 1911, with over 40,000 troops sent in; the Aube was then included in the zone
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Delimitation, AOC and ranking
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Per Comité Champagne, the 1927 law fixed the production area (about 34,200 ha) and permitted varieties, and the Champagne AOC was recognised in 1936. The village price scale (80–100%) dates from 1911, Grand/Premier Cru terms from 1952, and the scale was abolished in 2010 (details in Level 2)
slides.4.highlights.3.title: 2015: UNESCO World Heritage
slides.4.highlights.3.content: On 4 July 2015 "Champagne Hillsides, Houses and Cellars" was inscribed as a World Heritage Site, covering the historic vineyards of Hautvillers, Aÿ and Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, Saint-Nicaise hill in Reims, and Avenue de Champagne and Fort Chabrol in Épernay
slides.4.content: Sources often disagree on sequence (riots, delimitation, ranking), so rely on the Comité Champagne chronology and revisit it in the Level 2 regulation lesson.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
Which statement about Dom Pérignon best fits the historical record?
B. He presented the second-fermentation paper to the Royal Society in 1662
C. He was cellar master at Hautvillers Abbey, contributing to pressing and blending
Merret's paper predates his arrival and he did not invent the bubbles; his contribution was pressing, blending and quality.
In which year were "Champagne Hillsides, Houses and Cellars" inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list?
Inscribed on 4 July 2015; 1911 was the riots and 1936 the AOC.
Which dated record is most often cited as the first written description of sugar-induced second fermentation in bottle?
Merret presented to the Royal Society in 1662, before Dom Pérignon arrived in 1668.
